title: Research discovery lab
subtitle: Build a public route from your name or research question to the right paper, explanation, and source. Follow along with the talk, or work through the stations at your own pace.
permission: Add only the details you want to use during the lab. They stay in this browser. Skip any step that does not apply and come back later.
detailsNote: These details build direct links to your own public records. Leave anything blank that you do not have yet.

fields.label: Name you publish under
fields.hint: Used to build search links when you do not have an id yet.

fields.label: Institution or lab
fields.hint: Used for the lab-page and ROR checks.

fields.label: Your website
fields.hint: No trailing slash. Leave empty if you do not have one yet.

fields.label: ORCID iD
fields.hint: Digits and hyphens only. Paste the whole URL if that is easier.

fields.label: Google Scholar id
fields.hint: The user= value in your profile URL.

fields.label: Semantic Scholar author id
fields.hint: The number in your author page URL.

fields.label: OpenAlex author id
fields.hint: Starts with A. The ORCID lookup below finds it.

stations.name: Start with the records that identify you
stations.connection: Talk: slides 4–8 · Start with the records that identify you
stations.intro: Author records are often the first place a reader or search system encounters your work. Claim the records you use, correct the paper list, connect your website, then check the public view.

tasks.title: Check your public ORCID record
tasks.body: Open it while signed out. Confirm that the name, affiliation, works, and links you expect a reader to see are actually public.

tasks.title: Add the details that distinguish you
tasks.body: Use the name you publish under, your current affiliation, and your website. Set the visibility of each item to match what you want readers and indexing services to see.

tasks.title: Connect your works through DOI records
tasks.body: Use ORCID's Search and link tools or DOI records where possible, then check the imported title, authors, and DOI.

links.label: Works already tied to my ORCID

tasks.title: Claim and clean up your Semantic Scholar page
tasks.body: Find a paper you wrote, open the author page from your name, and claim it. Check both missing papers and papers that belong to someone else.

links.label: Search Semantic Scholar for my name

tasks.title: Check the OpenAlex record tied to your ORCID
tasks.body: Open the author record connected to your ORCID and compare its works with your publication list. Correct missing or misassigned work from the claimed profile.

links.label: Open the author record my ORCID resolves to

tasks.title: Make your Scholar profile useful as a public record
tasks.body: Make the profile public, verify your institutional email when eligible, and check the article list from a signed-out view.

tasks.title: Merge duplicate versions in Scholar
tasks.body: Look for preprint and published versions of the same paper on separate rows. Merge them when they represent the same work so the citation record stays together.

tasks.title: Check the page your institution or lab publishes about you
tasks.body: Confirm that it points to your current website and publication list and uses the name and affiliation you want readers to find.

links.label: Search for my name and institution

stations.name: Close the profile loop
stations.connection: Talk: slides 5 and 9 · The profile loop and the website
stations.intro: Your profiles identify the researcher; your website explains the work. Link them in both directions so a reader can move from an author record to your site and back.

tasks.title: Link your public records from your website
tasks.body: Put ORCID, Scholar, Semantic Scholar, and OpenAlex somewhere easy to find, such as the footer or about page.

tasks.title: Link your website from the records that support it
tasks.body: Add the website to ORCID, Scholar, and any other author profile that provides a homepage or researcher-URL field.

tasks.title: Walk the loop as a reader
tasks.body: Open a private window and move from a profile to your website and back. Check that the public pages and links are the ones you intended.

stations.name: Check crawling and indexing
stations.connection: Talk: slides 10–13 · Crawling, robots.txt, bots, and webmaster tools
stations.intro: Now check whether the website can be discovered and verified. Start with crawler access, then the sitemap and index controls, and finish in the webmaster tools.

tasks.title: Read your robots.txt as an access policy
tasks.body: Check which crawlers you allow, which paths you restrict, and which sitemap URLs you advertise. Use authentication for material that needs access control.

tasks.title: Check the sitemap
tasks.body: Confirm that it loads, lists the pages you care about, and is named in robots.txt. This gives crawlers a direct inventory of those URLs.

tasks.title: Check important pages for noindex
tasks.body: Inspect the pages you most want found for a robots meta tag or response header that prevents indexing.

tasks.title: Verify the site in Google Search Console
tasks.body: Add the property that matches your site and use a verification method you can keep deployed. For a github.io URL-prefix property, an HTML file or meta tag works.

tasks.title: Submit the sitemap and inspect one important page
tasks.body: Submit the sitemap, then use URL Inspection on a paper or concept page. Record what Google reports before changing the page.

tasks.title: Add the site to Bing Webmaster Tools
tasks.body: Import a verified Search Console property when available, then check the same sitemap and a representative page.

stations.name: Choose AI bot access
stations.connection: Talk: slides 11–12 · robots.txt and AI bot access
stations.intro: The talk separates search discovery, model training, and user-requested visits. Use robots.txt to record the access you want for each vendor and purpose.

tasks.title: Choose access by purpose
tasks.body: Review the documented bot names for the services you care about. Decide separately whether you want search discovery, training access, and user-requested visits.

tasks.title: Leave yourself a maintenance note
tasks.body: Add a short comment beside vendor-specific rules with the date and documentation you checked. This makes later updates much easier.

stations.name: Give readers a route into the ideas
stations.connection: Talk: slides 14–18 and 21 · Concept pages and public writing
stations.intro: A literature-review reader often starts with a problem or concept rather than a paper title. Give important ideas their own useful explanations and connect those explanations back to the evidence.

tasks.title: Choose one idea a reader might search for
tasks.body: Pick a term, procedure, failure mode, or design idea that matters to your work and can be understood without knowing the paper title.

tasks.title: Give the concept page a useful shape
tasks.body: State the idea, explain how it works in your research, describe the scope of the evidence, and point to the paper or protocol that supports it.

tasks.title: Explain why related pages connect
tasks.body: Link to another page when it helps the reader continue the idea. Use link text that tells them what they will find there.

tasks.title: Use a post for the reasoning around the research
tasks.body: Write about the example, decision, confusion, or open question that helps someone understand the work. Keep exploratory interpretations visibly exploratory.

stations.name: Test the public discovery route
stations.connection: Talk: slides 19–20 · Testing discovery with GenAI
stations.intro: Use an assistant the way a literature-review reader might. Save the prompt, answer, date, product, and cited URLs so you can compare the route after future changes.

tasks.title: Run the researcher test
tasks.body: Ask for a description of your work from public sources. Save which profiles and pages the answer uses.
tasks.prompt: Who is {name}, and what do they research? Cite the sources you used.

tasks.title: Run the topic test
tasks.body: Ask a research question in your area without naming yourself or the paper. Record whether your work appears and which source leads to it.
tasks.prompt: I am looking for recent work on <your topic>. What should I read, and who works on it? Cite sources.

tasks.title: Run the website test
tasks.body: Give the assistant your site and ask what it thinks you work on, which pages it used, and what it could not resolve from the public text.
tasks.prompt: Read {site} and summarise what this researcher works on. Which pages did you use, and what is missing or wrong?

tasks.title: Check the answer against the source
tasks.body: Confirm that the generated description preserves the scope, status, and evidence of the work it cites. Record any overstatement or missing context.

stations.name: Measure and maintain the route
stations.intro: Keep a small repeatable record. Each new publication or explanation becomes a trigger to check the public route once, fix what changed, and move on.

tasks.title: Keep a one-page discovery log
tasks.body: Record the question, date, product, answer, cited URL, and whether the answer represented the source accurately.

tasks.title: Use publication and writing changes as triggers
tasks.body: After a publication or profile change, check the DOI record, profiles, paper page, and CV. After a new concept page or post, add the relevant links and rerun the same discovery check.

discussion.name: Bring these questions to the discussion
items: What profile record would you fix first?
Which concept page would help a literature-review reader?
What should count as a useful GEO check?
Where should robots.txt be permissive, and where restrictive?
